hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
I would not currently inject gray-market “research peptides.” The sourcing and quality-control risks are simply too high.

The question isn’t whether peptides can work as signaling molecules (they can). It’s whether the vial contains the peptide it claims, at the stated dose, without microbial contamination, endotoxins, heavy metals, or peptide-related impurities.

The FDA does not verify the safety, effectiveness, or quality of compounded drugs before marketing. Does that mean every compounded product is unsafe? No. But the safeguards are different.

Until a specific research peptide has credible human evidence and a reliable source with transparent, independent testing, I would hold off.

hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
Bone health deserves attention before menopause, not just after.

Roughly two-thirds of bone lost across the menopausal transition tends to occur within a three-year window - from one year before to two years after the final menstrual period.

In a study of 862 women, bone density at the spine fell 10.6% over 10 years, but 7.4% was lost during this brief “transmenopause” period. Bone density of the femur fell 9.1%, with 5.8% lost during the same window.

This is a reason for women to prioritize resistance and high-impact training around the menopause transition to prevent or slow the loss of bone density.

hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
Exercise slowed epigenetic aging on two DNA-methylation clocks in breast cancer survivors.

During the first 6 months of the 12-month study, epigenetic aging halted in the exercise group while controls aged at twice the chronological rate, even though the intervention added only about 6 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity per day!

Faster epigenetic aging was also associated with worse attention and self-reported cognition, and some methylation changes implicated BDNF signaling as a plausible link to neuroplasticity.

This suggests some aging signatures after cancer treatment appear to be responsive to movement, even when the added activity isn't enormous.

hits.name: Andy Galpin, PhD
hits.text:
Why wouldn't you want your testosterone as high as possible? Dr. Ben House has a good answer.

High testosterone upregulates EPO, which tells your body to make more red blood cells. More red blood cells means more viscous blood. You're not pumping blood anymore, you're pumping oil.

Now add left ventricular hypertrophy. The heart wall thickens, and it's pushing against more back pressure with every beat.

As Ben puts it, your heart is pumping ketchup against a bunch of extra muscle.

You don't want to run that for decades, assuming you get decades.

hits.name: David Sinclair
Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
It’s a reality of aging that we need more dietary protein to keep muscle mass. If you're over 65, the source of your protein may matter as much as the amount.

Researchers gave older adults two meals with the same amount of protein and the same calories. One was built around beef, and the other was vegan. After the beef meal, muscle protein synthesis was about 47% higher. After the vegan meal, it barely moved from where it was before eating (PMID 37972895).

As we age, muscle gets harder to build and easier to lose. We need to make high-quality animal protein the anchor of every meal.

hits.name: Nick Norwitz MD PhD
hits.text:
“Let Me Tell You About My Grift”

A physician recently published a post using AI to analyze 12 health influencers and their supposed “grifts.”

The individual is not worth platforming, but this it provides a useful springboard for a bigger conversation.

The medical and informational ecosystems are evolving, creating a new niche for professional scientific communicators.

If you watch the video below (10 minutes), you’ll see I’ve been transparent about why I’ve made the decisions I’ve made.

My path was shaped by my own health story and a belief that I can do more good by educating people and empowering them on their health journeys than by writing prescriptions.

But as this ecosystem evolves, some conventional clinicians seem uncomfortable that their professional influence is undermined by media educators. I’ve even had one old scholar cardiologist call me on the phone to complain “my patients are asking hard questions.”

“Sorry?” I guess 

But find it ironic when a clinician uses AI to label me a "grifter," with the precise claim being that I have a YouTube with 1.3 million subscribers and a paid newsletter.

But I’ll do them one better.

Let me tell you about my grift.

Yes, I have a paid newsletter. #StayCurious Metabolism has become a top premium science newsletters on Substack. In 2026, we’ve held the #1 Rising Science position more often than every other science newsletter on the platform combined.

Subscriptions start at the “hefty” price of $8 per month (less than 67 cents per letter).

Why do people pay?

Judging by comments from my community, it’s because the information gives them knowledge and tools to take greater control of their health; to understand their biology and approach conversations with physicians as informed partners rather than passive objects to be “compliant.”

But here’s something else you might like to know.

I’ve repeatedly turned down substantial financial offers (including six-figure deals) from companies whose products I didn’t believe in or organizations I wasn’t comfortable affiliating with, including pharmaceutical companies.

I could have taken enough money from pharma to put a down payment on a house.

I didn’t. Not a cent.

My friends and colleagues can attest to that, and to the fact that I’ve been brutally transparent about my own health journey, even when doing so put my reputation at risk. 

I’m doing what I’m doing not because it’s the easy path, but because I believe it’s the path where I can make the biggest impact.

I don’t say that to put myself above anyone else. As you’ll see in the video below, my entire social ecosystem is in medicine. And to me, these people are heroes. We need good clinicians.

But there is a particular species of small, bitter clinician who comes online primarily to take shots at other people.

My advice to them is simple: focus on being a great clinician.

And if you’re going to get on the internet, focus on contributing something intellectually valuable.

Because taking potshots at people who chose a different path isn’t intellectual contribution. It’s just a transparent signal that you want to be a thought “influencer” … but you’re not very good.

And at the end of the day, the insecure medical bullies remind me exactly why I do what I do. Because patients need power. And paternalistic medicine needs to die.

The 'Shroom I'm Eating for Brain Health ‍

1/3) Every once in a while, I read a paper that actually changes what ends up on my dinner plate. This was one of those papers, recently published in Nature Aging. 

And the food in question is a mushroom, a particular one.

But let’s start with a nutrient: Ergothioneine.

Ergothioneine is a sulfur-containing amino acid with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties.

Interestingly, its levels also decline with age, paralleling the gradual loss of antioxidant defenses that occurs as we get older.

In fact, some researchers have even proposed classifying ergothioneine as a “longevity vitamin” or “stress vitamin.”

outsiders.name: Andrej Karpathy
outsiders.text:
We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks:

Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better:

Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better:

Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better:

Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work!

In summary:
- As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding.
- Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.

outsiders.name: Anthropic
outsiders.text:
In physics, an “impedance mismatch” occurs when two systems each work well but are poorly matched.

In this Science Blog guest post, Harvard physicist Matthew Schwartz argues that something similar is happening with AI and science. LLMs are capable at many things, but working with them as you would with a human collaborator isn’t currently the best way to elicit their scientific strengths.

To address this mismatch, Schwartz created a toolkit for exact calculations in quantitative science. Because similar calculations often emerge in very different areas of science, Claude found connections to ecology, population genetics, and a dozen other fields, and Schwartz worked with domain experts to steer it towards interesting questions.

Read more about these projects here:
